title: Transaction Isolation Levels & Concurrency Anomalies
description: Compare Read Committed, Repeatable Read, and Serializable levels, and prevent Dirty Reads, Non-Repeatable Reads, and Serialization Anomaly.

data.text: SQL defines four isolation levels that dictate what concurrency anomalies are permitted. Because of PostgreSQL's MVCC design, **Dirty Reads are physically impossible** at every isolation level.
Concurrency Anomalies vs Isolation Levels in PostgreSQL

The differences between the levels only show up with two concurrent transactions. In `READ COMMITTED`, each statement takes a fresh snapshot, so a second read can see rows committed by another transaction after the first read. In `REPEATABLE READ`, the snapshot is taken once at the first statement and reused, so the same query returns the same rows for the life of the transaction.

data.title: Repeatable Read sees a stable snapshot
data.content: In session 1, the second SELECT returns the same total even though session 2 committed an insert in between. The same sequence under READ COMMITTED would show the new row.

data.title: SERIALIZABLE requires retries
data.text: `SERIALIZABLE` prevents serialization anomalies by aborting transactions that would produce a result impossible under serial execution, raising SQLSTATE `40001`. Correct application code must catch that error and retry the whole transaction. If your code has no retry loop, raising the isolation level does not buy safety — it just converts a subtle bug into a visible error.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: PostgreSQL defaults to `READ COMMITTED` (each statement sees rows committed before statement start).
`REPEATABLE READ` takes a transaction-level snapshot at the start of the transaction.
`SERIALIZABLE` utilizes Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI) to prevent write skew.
